title: The Nurse of Calcutta and the God of the Witches: Egypt, Malta, and the Religion That Was Not There
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Calcutta, birth in the mill manager's house
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date given in the sources
stops.campa: In the colonial city on the Hooghly a daughter is born to James Murray, manager in the Serampore paper mills, and to his wife Margaret Carr, who came out to India as a missionary six years before. They name her Margaret Alice. An older sister, Mary, is already in the house; a paternal grandmother and a great-grandmother complete it. Her first years run on ships and stations between two hemispheres, and no house in either of them stays hers for long. Fifty-four years on, Annie Besant will preside over the Indian National Congress in this same city.
suggested_refs: The Serampore paper mills on the Hooghly, where James Murray worked

stops.name: Lambourn, the vicarage of uncle John
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: At seven she is sent to England with Mary and lodged in the Berkshire vicarage of her uncle John and his wife Harriet, while the parents stay in India. It is the ordinary arithmetic of empire: the children go home, home being a country they have not lived in. The uncle walks them out to the local monuments, the barrows and standing stones of the downs, and the girl who will spend her life opening other people's graves is shown her first one here. Her mother is on the other side of the world. The arrangement holds for three years.
suggested_refs: The prehistoric monuments of the Lambourn Downs, shown to her by her uncle

stops.name: Bonn, schooling in German
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Her mother collects the girls and takes them across to the Rhine. In Bonn the two sisters are schooled and come out fluent in German, a second European language Margaret keeps for the rest of her life and uses, half a century on, when German scholarship on folklore and witchcraft crosses her desk. She is ten years old and has now lived in three countries. Bonn is a middle station between the Calcutta she was born in and the England she is being made into, and the schooling there lasts two years.
suggested_refs: The German schooling of 1873-1875, source of her reading knowledge of continental folklore scholarship

stops.name: Sydenham, the merchant household
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: After two further years in Calcutta the family lands for good in the London suburbs, and James Murray works from the firm's London office. Sydenham gives Margaret her first long stretch of settled English life: a merchant household in a street of merchant households, one Anglo-Indian family among the thousands the imperial economy shuttles between its two poles. She is fourteen, out of school, and no profession is open to a girl of her class in that street. Seventeen years pass between this address and the university enrolment that finally gives her a trade.
suggested_refs: The Anglo-Indian merchant colony of south London in the 1870s

stops.name: Calcutta General Hospital, seven years of nursing
stops.date_confidence: contradiction in the pool, not resolved: the chronology lens dates this 1883, the geography lens 1880-1887; the source text reads 'In 1880, they returned to Calcutta, where Margaret remained for the next seven years', so 1880 is used here and the disagreement is recorded
stops.campa: She is back in Bengal, and for seven years she nurses at the Calcutta General Hospital, run by the Anglican Sisterhood of Clewer, through a city where cholera is a season rather than an event. The work is bodies: wounds dressed, the dead handled, bone under the hand as ordinary matter. Thirty years on she will unwrap a mummy in front of five hundred people in a Manchester lecture theatre without a tremor, and she will read the anatomy in witch-trial confessions the way a nurse reads a chart.
suggested_refs: The Calcutta General Hospital under the Anglican Sisterhood of Clewer, and the cholera outbreak she nursed through

stops.name: Bushey Heath, the father's death
stops.date_confidence: year of the death attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Home from India at twenty-four, she takes up the charitable work expected of an unmarried woman of her class, first at Rugby in Warwickshire, then in the Hertfordshire house she keeps for her retired father. James Murray dies there in 1891. The household dissolves with him. She is twenty-eight, unmarried, with no profession and no training, and for the first time in her life nobody else's posting decides where she lives. Two years later she sails to Madras to see her sister.
suggested_refs: The Rugby social work of 1887 and the Bushey Heath household kept for James Murray

stops.name: Madras, the last Indian crossing
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: She sails once more to India to visit her sister at Madras. It is her last documented crossing to the subcontinent. Thirty years of shuttling between two hemispheres end here, and no source records anything of the visit itself. Down the coast at Adyar the Theosophical Society keeps its world headquarters, where Annie Besant will settle and rule; the two women never meet, and both will be read long afterwards as tributaries of the same conviction, that an older religion survives underneath the official one. Murray goes home to London and enrols in a university.
suggested_refs: The Theosophical Society headquarters at Adyar, near Madras

segments.name: Gower Street and the Egyptian Seasons, 1894-1908

stops.name: University College London, enrolment at thirty
stops.date_confidence: month attested (January 1894); day not recorded, defaulted to the 1st
stops.campa: At thirty, with no degree and no training of any kind, she walks into University College London and enrols to study Egyptology under Flinders Petrie. It is an improbably late start and it takes at once. Within a year she is publishing on the descent of property in early Egypt; within four she is a junior lecturer, the first woman to hold an archaeology lecturing post in Britain. Gower Street becomes the fixed pole of the next four decades, the address she returns to between seasons in the field.
suggested_refs: 'The Descent of Property in the Early Periods of Egyptian History' (1895), her first academic paper

stops.name: Abydos, the Osireion under the sand
stops.date_confidence: season attested to 1902; the excavation ran across 1902-1903 and no start date is recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: In Petrie's excavation season at Abydos she works the ground behind the temple of Seti and helps uncover the Osireion, the sunken hall of hewn granite built for the cult of Osiris, its floor standing in Nile water. She publishes it in 1904 under her own name. The nurse from the Calcutta General is now an excavator at Abydos, a burial ground already in use under the first dynasties. Fifty-three years earlier Gustave Flaubert came ashore at Alexandria wanting the Orient that Bonaparte's campaign taught France to want, and went up this same river to look at it.
suggested_refs: Margaret A. Murray, 'The Osireion at Abydos' (1904)

stops.name: Saqqara, the mastaba season
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: The next season is the Old Kingdom cemetery south of Cairo: mastaba tombs cleared, recorded, published as Saqqara Mastabas. It is unglamorous work, pottery and bone logged where they lie, the discipline of moving nothing until it is written down. She will spend the second half of her life arguing from evidence handled in exactly the opposite way: scattered trial confessions lifted out of three centuries and four countries and set side by side as though they were one stratum.
suggested_refs: Margaret A. Murray, 'Saqqara Mastabas I' (1905)

stops.name: Cairo, the apparatus of the savants
stops.date_confidence: inferred: her Egyptian seasons ran through the Cairo permit and antiquities apparatus, but no source dates a specific stay in the city
stops.campa: The permits, the antiquities service, the dealers, the whole apparatus her seasons pass through has its offices in Cairo. Bonaparte founded the Institut d'Egypte here in 1798 with Joseph Fourier as its secretary and Pierre-Francois Bouchard among the officers who fed it, and the European excavation of Egypt has been one continuous institution ever since. Helena Blavatsky opened her Societe Spirite in this city in 1871 and closed it inside the year. Rene Guenon will come ashore in 1930 and never leave. Murray is a visitor here; she always goes home.
suggested_refs: The Institut d'Egypte, founded 22 August 1798, ancestor of the excavation apparatus Murray worked within

stops.name: Manchester Museum, the unwrapping of Khnum-nakht
stops.date_confidence: month attested (May 1908); day not recorded, defaulted to the 1st
stops.campa: She has been coming to Manchester since 1906 to catalogue Petrie's Egyptian material and to lecture, and in May she unwraps the mummy of Khnum-nakht in the museum in front of an audience of more than five hundred. No woman has led a public unwrapping before. The linen comes off in public, and the event makes her a name outside the lecture halls. The book on the two brothers of the tomb follows in 1910. No curse story attaches to the event in any reachable source.
suggested_refs: The Two Brothers, Khnum-nakht and Nakht-Ankh, in the Manchester Museum collection

stops.name: London, the journal Ancient Egypt
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Petrie founds a journal called Ancient Egypt and Murray runs it, de facto editor of a quarterly she will still be editing under a different name twenty years later. Then the war takes the university apart. She enrols as a volunteer nurse, the trade she learned in Calcutta thirty-five years before, and works at it until illness pulls her out. She is fifty-one. The Egyptology does not stop. In 1915, in the gap the war opens, she begins reading the records of the European witch trials.
suggested_refs: The journal Ancient Egypt, founded by Petrie in 1914 and edited in practice by Murray

stops.name: Glastonbury, convalescence among the legends
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the wartime stay at Glastonbury is attested but undated within the war years, and the causal link to her witchcraft work is inference, not testimony
stops.campa: Sent to Somerset to recover, she is set down in the one English town that keeps its own mythology in working order: the thorn, the abbey, Arthur's supposed grave, a folklore still being told rather than filed. She reads and she listens. By the end of the war she is working from a proposition: that the confessions extracted at the witch trials record something the witnesses had actually seen, and that the Devil in them is a man in a mask standing in front of a congregation.
stops.quote: When I suddenly realised that the so-called Devil was simply a disguised man I was startled, almost alarmed, by the way the recorded facts fell into place, and showed that the witches were members of an old and primitive form of religion, and the records had been made by members of a new and persecuting form.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Margaret Murray, My First Hundred Years (William Kimber, 1963), seen only at second hand through Wikipedia's citation; the memoir itself was not fetched
suggested_refs: Glastonbury Abbey and the living folklore of the town during the First World War

stops.name: London, the first article in Folklore
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Her first article on the witch-cult appears in Folklore: the accused of the early modern trials were neither deluded nor invented but the surviving practitioners of a pre-Christian fertility religion, organised in covens under a horned god their persecutors called the Devil. A second article follows in 1920. Within a mile of her desk, Arthur Edward Waite is tracing the real textual pedigree of rituals other men call ancient, and Theodor Reuss is selling a lineage for his own order. The three of them are working in one city in one decade, in opposite directions.
stops.quote: He was a meikle black roch man. Sometimes he had boots and sometimes shoes on his foot; but still [always] his foot are forked and cloven.
stops.quote_source: Confession of Isobel Gowdie, Auldearne, 1662, as quoted by Murray in The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921); the bracketed gloss is Murray's own. Project Gutenberg edition 20411
suggested_refs: Margaret Murray's 1917 and 1920 articles in the journal Folklore

stops.name: Oxford, the Clarendon Press prints the witch-cult
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Oxford University Press publishes The Witch-Cult in Western Europe, refereed for the press by the folklorist Henry Balfour. The method is stated without embarrassment: trial confessions are read as testimony about what the accused actually did, and the circumstances under which they were extracted are set aside. Scotland, the Basque country, Essex and Lorraine are laid side by side as one religion. The book sells about two thousand copies in thirty years, then becomes a bestseller in the 1950s, which is what finally provokes the historians into taking it apart.
stops.quote: The subject of Witches and Witchcraft has always suffered from the biassed opinions of the commentators, both contemporary and of later date.
stops.quote_source: Margaret A. Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1921), opening sentence of the Introduction; Internet Archive full-text scan witchcultinweste21murr
suggested_refs: The Clarendon Press first edition of The Witch-Cult in Western Europe, 1921

stops.name: University College London, assistant professor
stops.date_confidence: year of the promotion attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Lecturer in 1921, senior lecturer in 1922, assistant professor of Egyptology in 1924: she rises through Gower Street on the Egyptology while the witchcraft goes out under the same name and the same institutional address. In her own mind there is no separation between them. She has a department, a journal, an honorary doctorate coming in 1927, and the Folklore Society. The Egyptology pays for the address the witchcraft is written from. She is sixty-one, with thirty-nine years of work still in front of her.
stops.quote: Ritual Witchcraft, or, as I propose to call it, the Dianic cult, embraces the religious beliefs and ritual of the people known in late mediaeval times as 'Witches'.
stops.quote_source: Margaret A. Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (Clarendon Press, 1921), Introduction, the Ritual Witchcraft passage; Project Gutenberg edition 20411
suggested_refs: The UCL Egyptology department under Petrie and Murray in the 1920s

stops.name: Valletta, into the Grand Harbour
stops.date_confidence: the Malta campaign is attested as beginning in 1921; no arrival date is recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: She comes into the Grand Harbour to begin seven years of Maltese seasons, run as teaching digs for British students between terms at UCL. It is the harbour the Knights of Saint John surrendered to Bonaparte's fleet in 1798, with Joseph Fourier aboard and Pierre-Francois Bouchard a week at anchor; the island they handed over sits on a megalithic architecture older than the pyramids Bouchard's column marched past at Imbaba. Which Maltese sites Murray took in which season the sources do not agree on.
suggested_refs: The Grand Harbour of Valletta, surrendered by the Knights of Saint John in June 1798

stops.name: Borg in-Nadur, the Bronze Age walls
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: the geography lens gives a single 1923 season, the site's own record gives 1922-1927 for her investigation of the main temple area; the span is used and the disagreement recorded. Coordinate corrected from 35.8283/14.5219, which was about 0.7 km off
stops.campa: Above Marsaxlokk Bay she digs the Bronze Age site of Borg in-Nadur, clearing the fortification wall and the hut floors of Malta's later prehistory. The excavation is published and cited on its own terms, with no bearing on the witch-cult argument running in London at the same time. The dates given for her seasons here differ from source to source, one naming a single year and another the whole span to 1927. She is nearly sixty and directing the trench herself.
suggested_refs: The fortification wall and hut remains of Borg in-Nadur, above Marsaxlokk Bay

stops.name: Ghar Dalam, the cave sequence at Birzebbuga
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: her work here is reported only in accounts of the Maltese campaign and is undated within 1921-1927; the cave's own record does not name her. Coordinate corrected from 35.8494/14.5286, which was about 1.4 km north of the cave
stops.campa: The deep cave at Birzebbuga holds the sequence: Ice Age fauna in the lower beds, human occupation above, one of the key stratigraphies of the Mediterranean. Issel dug it in 1865 and Cooke in 1892, and the cave's own record does not name Murray at all; her involvement comes from accounts of her Maltese seasons rather than from the site. She works it, on that testimony, as one station of the campaign, and teaches students to read a section while she is there. The cave keeps the older names.
suggested_refs: The Pleistocene and Neolithic beds of Ghar Dalam, excavated by Issel in 1865 and Cooke in 1892

stops.name: Whomerle Wood, the homestead moat
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Between the Mediterranean campaigns she runs a volunteer excavation of the Homestead Moat earthwork in the wood outside Stevenage, a small English dig worked by amateurs she is training. It is the smallest dig of her career: in the same summer that her horned god is being read in London drawing rooms, she is in a Hertfordshire wood putting a section through a ditch. The same ground is her field site and her evidence, and no other archaeologist finds the religion in it.
suggested_refs: The Homestead Moat earthwork in Whomerle Wood, near Stevenage

stops.name: London, the Encyclopaedia Britannica entry
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: She writes the entry on witchcraft for the Encyclopaedia Britannica, and writes it as settled fact: the cult, the covens, the god, set before every household and school library that owns the edition as the state of scholarly knowledge. The entry stands until 1968. For nearly forty years anyone in the English-speaking world who looks up witchcraft in the reference of record reads Margaret Murray, and does not read that any historian disagrees. That same year she sails to South Africa for the meeting of the British Association.
suggested_refs: The 'Witchcraft' entry in the Encyclopaedia Britannica, in print from 1929 until 1968

stops.name: Trepuco, the talaiot outside Mahon
stops.date_confidence: campaign attested to 1930-1931, with the taula precinct cleared in 1931; no season start date recorded, defaulted to 1 January 1930. Coordinate corrected from 39.8814/4.2447, which was about 1.9 km off
stops.campa: On Menorca she excavates the talaiotic settlement outside Mahon: the great dry-stone tower, the enclosure, the taula whose precinct she clears in 1931. It is the last campaign of Mediterranean fieldwork she directs in person; after Menorca she works through other hands and through print. She is sixty-seven. The tower still stands on the site much as her season left it exposed, and the Balearic seasons close ten years of fieldwork in the western Mediterranean.
suggested_refs: The talaiot and taula of Trepuco, near Mahon, Menorca

stops.name: London, Sampson Low prints The God of the Witches
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January. Some accounts give 1933 for the printing
stops.campa: Sampson Low publishes The God of the Witches, the same thesis stripped of its apparatus and written for everybody: a horned god worshipped continuously in England from before Christianity to the seventeenth century, the trials a persecution rather than a delusion. This is the book that travels. Gerald Gardner reads it, says in 1939 that he has found a surviving coven in the New Forest, and builds Wicca on the frame; the word the sources use is blueprint. She will be called, later, the grandmother of Wicca.
stops.quote: The evidence proves that underlying the Christian religion was a cult practised by many classes of the community, chiefly, however, by the more ignorant or those in the less thickly inhabited parts of the country. It can be traced back to pre-Christian times, and appears to be the ancient religion of Western Europe.
stops.quote_source: Margaret A. Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (Clarendon Press, 1921), Introduction, immediately following the Dianic cult definition; Project Gutenberg edition 20411. Quoted whole here because the version in circulation cuts a clause and a sentence boundary with a single ellipsis
suggested_refs: The God of the Witches (Sampson Low, 1931), the book Gerald Gardner built on

stops.name: Leningrad, the Soviet collections
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the sources say only 'the early 1930s' and fix no year; 1932 is a placement within that span, not an attested date
stops.campa: She tours the museums of the Soviet Union, Leningrad and Moscow, Kharkov and Kiev, at a moment when a British scholar walking into Soviet collections is itself a political event. What she saw and whom she met is recorded nowhere reachable; the trip is attested and empty. She is approaching seventy and travelling through a country most of her colleagues will never enter. Back in London she takes over Petrie's journal on his retirement and renames it Ancient Egypt and the East.
suggested_refs: The Soviet museum circuit of the early 1930s: Leningrad, Moscow, Kharkov, Kiev

stops.name: Girton College, Cambridge, the catalogue
stops.date_confidence: start year attested; the cataloguing ran to 1940 and the Cambridge lectures to 1942, two spans the pool had conflated. Coordinate corrected from 52.2189/0.0866, about 1.1 km south of the college
stops.campa: At Cambridge she takes on the Egyptian antiquities of Girton College, cataloguing the collection object by object from 1934 to 1940 and lecturing in the university until 1942. The two spans are quoted as one in most accounts, and they are not one: the catalogue ends in 1940, the lectures run two years past it. She is seventy-one when she starts, and she is editing Ancient Egypt and the East out of London through the same years. The college gives her a second base outside the capital, and it is where she spends the war once the bombing starts.
suggested_refs: The Egyptian antiquities collection of Girton College, catalogued by Murray from 1934

stops.name: University College London, the retirement
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: She retires from the assistant professorship at seventy-two, forty-one years after walking into the same building with no qualification of any kind. The retirement ends the post and nothing else. She keeps the journal and the Folklore Society, goes on lecturing, and within months is on a ship for Palestine to dig. What Gower Street keeps of her is a bust in the Institute of Archaeology and a common room for women named after her, which she had to campaign to get built.
suggested_refs: The Margaret Murray Room at UCL, the women's common room she campaigned for

stops.name: Jerusalem, at the Petries' base
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: the geography lens dated this stay 'from 1933', the source places it after the 1935 retirement; 1935 is used and the disagreement recorded. Month not attested
stops.campa: Petrie has moved his operation to Palestine and Murray follows to assist, staying in Jerusalem through the last years he is still working. Forty-one years after she enrolled as his student the arrangement is unchanged in form: he digs, she works alongside him. The dates given for the stay differ between accounts, some putting it as early as 1933 and others only after her retirement. She has now worked at both the Egyptian and the Levantine ends of the same excavation world.
suggested_refs: The Petries' Palestine base of operations in the 1930s

stops.name: Tell el-Ajjul, the last mound
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month not recorded, placed after the Jerusalem stay
stops.campa: At the Bronze Age mound near Gaza she takes her last season of Middle Eastern fieldwork, both of them in their seventies, the teacher and the student of 1894 still on one site. The mound yields rich Bronze Age material. It closes a working partnership that has run forty-one years, through Abydos, Saqqara, a journal, a department, and a theory about English witches that Petrie never had to answer for. She goes home to England and almost immediately leaves again.
suggested_refs: Petrie's excavation of the Bronze Age mound at Tall al-Ajjul, near Gaza

stops.name: Oslo, the lecture circuit begins
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'late 1935'; October is a placement within that, not a recorded date
stops.campa: At seventy-two she starts a lecture tour of the north: Oslo first, then Sweden, Finland and Estonia, carrying Egyptology and folklore into capitals she has never worked in. She travels without institutional escort. The itinerary is attested and the contents of the lectures are not; what survives is the itinerary itself, and the fact that a woman of seventy-two crossed northern Europe in winter to keep it. Within five years the war closes every route on this itinerary and Estonia has stopped existing as a state.
suggested_refs: The Scandinavian and Baltic lecture tour of late 1935

stops.name: Helsinki, the same season
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'late 1935'; November is a placement in the sequence of the tour, not a recorded date
stops.campa: The circuit runs on to Helsinki, one Nordic capital after another inside a few weeks. What she said in the hall is recorded nowhere reachable. The Finnish Literature Society keeps its folk-poetry archive in this city, one of the largest collections of oral tradition anywhere in Europe, and a folklorist of her standing is in town; whether she went into that archive is not stated in any source consulted. She is seventy-two and the tour has two more countries to run.
suggested_refs: The Finnish Literature Society folklore archive, contemporary with her visit

stops.name: Tallinn, the far end of the itinerary
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'late 1935'; December is the tour's closing leg by sequence, not a recorded date
stops.campa: The tour's last leg crosses to Tallinn, the farthest north and east she is documented as travelling. Estonia in 1935 is an independent republic with five years left to it. She lectures, and goes home to England, and the Baltic drops out of her itinerary and out of most of Europe's for the next fifteen years. It is the last foreign lecture tour of her life. She has dug on three continents and has been crossing between England and Bengal, or England and the Mediterranean, since she was seven.
suggested_refs: Independent Estonia in 1935, the last stop of her Baltic circuit

stops.name: Petra, the cave dwellings at seventy-three
stops.date_confidence: month attested (March 1937, running into April); day not recorded, defaulted to the 1st
stops.campa: At seventy-three she directs an excavation of the cave dwellings at Petra, the Nabataean city cut into the sandstone of the Transjordanian hills, working the rock-cut houses rather than the famous facades. Petrie, ten years her senior, has five years left to live. This is the last dig she personally directs abroad and the last time the pattern set at Abydos in 1902 repeats itself entire: the season, the workmen, the notebook, the publication. She has been digging for thirty-five years.
suggested_refs: The rock-cut cave dwellings of Petra, excavated by Murray in the spring of 1937

segments.name: The War and the Bloomsbury Room, 1939-1957

stops.name: Cambridge, evacuated from the Blitz
stops.date_confidence: the wartime Cambridge base is attested for 1939-1945; the month is the war's opening, not a recorded arrival
stops.campa: The bombing drives her out of London and she spends the war based at Cambridge, finishing the Girton catalogue in 1940 and volunteering to teach service personnel billeted through the colleges in their thousands. She is seventy-six when it starts and eighty-two when it ends. The lecture circuit is gone and the journal's readership with it, and most of her contemporaries are dead. No source records what she was paid for the Cambridge teaching, or whether she was paid at all. She is at a desk with objects on it for the duration.
suggested_refs: The wartime colleges of Cambridge, where she taught military personnel

stops.name: Hagley Wood, the woman in the wych elm
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the consultation is reported rather than documented, the exact wording of her answer is preserved nowhere, and the coordinate is taken from the site, the pool having given none
stops.campa: A woman's skeleton has been found inside a hollow wych elm in the Worcestershire wood, a hand buried apart from the body, and graffiti is appearing on walls across the Midlands asking who put Bella down the wych elm. Murray is consulted and reportedly answers with ritual murder: the hand, the tree, an occult killing. The case is never solved. The consultation is thinly sourced and nothing she actually said survives, and the story fastens itself to her name permanently.
suggested_refs: The unsolved 'Bella in the Wych Elm' case, Hagley Wood, Worcestershire

stops.name: Endsleigh Street, the bedsit in Bloomsbury
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'post-1945'; 1946 is a placement within that, not a recorded date
stops.campa: After the war she takes a bedsitting room in Bloomsbury, a few minutes' walk from University College and the Institute of Archaeology, and lives there in one room. Every formal appointment is finished. She stays inside the radius of the buildings that trained her at thirty, and teaches ancient Egyptian history twice a week to adult-education classes at the City Literary Institute, into her eighties and then her nineties. The witch-cult books are selling to a readership she never meets; the Egyptology is taught to twenty people at a time in an evening class.
suggested_refs: Her adult-education classes on ancient Egypt at the City Literary Institute

stops.name: London, president of the Folklore Society
stops.date_confidence: presidency attested 1953-1955; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: At ninety she becomes president of the Folklore Society, taking the chair after Allan Gomme's resignation and holding it two years. The society is the institutional home the witch-cult thesis has, Egyptology having quietly declined to house it. She has been a member since 1927. In 1960 she donates her papers to its archive, and in 1961 the society's journal gives an entire autumn issue over to a Festschrift for her ninety-eighth birthday. She is ninety-two when she gives the chair up.
stops.quote: I have not attempted to disentangle the various cults; I am content merely to point out that it was a definite religion with beliefs, ritual, and organization as highly developed as that of any other cult in the world.
stops.quote_source: Margaret A. Murray, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921), Introduction, closing the Ritual Witchcraft and Dianic cult passage; Project Gutenberg edition 20411
suggested_refs: The Murray papers in the Folklore Society Archive, deposited 1960

stops.name: London, The Divine King in England
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: She publishes The Divine King in England, which extends the thesis to its end: that several English kings died as ritual sacrifices to the old religion, killed on a cycle by their own people. The academic world does not argue with the book so much as look away from it. The same year Gerald Gardner publishes Witchcraft Today, and the religion built on her framework walks out into public English life at the moment the history behind it is being abandoned.
stops.quote: thow saw Christsonday cum out of the snaw in liknes of a staig
stops.quote_source: Confession of Andro Man, Aberdeen witch trials, 1597, as quoted by Murray in The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921); Project Gutenberg edition 20411
suggested_refs: The Divine King in England (1954) and Gardner's Witchcraft Today (1954), published the same year

stops.name: Wandlebury, the hill-figures that are not there
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 1 January. Coordinate is the Wandlebury ring, the pool having given none
stops.campa: At ninety-four she comes out publicly for T. C. Lethbridge, who claims to have located giant figures cut into the chalk of the Cambridgeshire ring and recovered them by sounding the ground with an iron bar. Professional archaeology rejects the figures. Murray champions them in print regardless, having spent forty years reading the English landscape for survivals she is already certain are in it. It is the same disagreement her witch-cult has been having with the historians since 1921.
suggested_refs: T. C. Lethbridge's disputed hill-figures at Wandlebury, Cambridgeshire

stops.name: North Finchley, the house of retired nurses
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'early 1960s'; 1961 is a placement before the documented 1962 move into full-time care
stops.campa: In extreme old age she moves into a North Finchley house run by retired nurses, the last address where she lives without full-time care. She began her working life nursing at the Calcutta General Hospital in 1880, dressing wounds through a cholera season, and ends it in the keeping of the same trade eighty years later. She is ninety-eight and still lecturing when she can be got to a hall. What she does with the days in this house is recorded nowhere; the address is attested and the life inside it is not.
suggested_refs: The North Finchley home run by retired nurses, her last independent address

stops.name: Welwyn, the hundredth birthday
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date; coordinate corrected to Welwyn village from 51.8112/-0.2094, which falls south toward Welwyn Garden City, a different settlement
stops.campa: She turns a hundred in Hertfordshire, under twenty-four-hour nursing care, and marks it with two books: The Genesis of Religion, and My First Hundred Years, the autobiography, which the reviewers treat kindly. A party is held and she sits through it enthroned. Petrie has been dead twenty-one years, and most of the scholars who first doubted her are dead too. The religion built on her thesis is nine years into public life in England, and she is alive to see it.
stops.quote: [I] went to her hundredth birthday party where she sat enthroned—no other word for it—surrounded by family and friends
stops.quote_source: Glyn Daniel, 'Editorial', Antiquity 38, no. 149 (1964): 1-6, at p. 2; seen at second hand through Wikipedia's pull-quote, and given here with the original em dashes rather than restyled
suggested_refs: My First Hundred Years (William Kimber, 1963) and The Genesis of Religion (1963)

stops.name: Welwyn, death at the Queen Victoria Memorial Hospital
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date; same coordinate correction as the previous stop
stops.campa: She dies at the Queen Victoria Memorial Hospital four months after the hundredth birthday, a century and four months after being born in Calcutta. Nearly every colleague of the Petrie generation is long dead. Her Britannica entry is still in print and will stand another five years. Her books are selling better than they ever sold in her working life, and the historians are about to begin taking the witch-cult thesis apart. She has been a published author for sixty-eight years.
stops.quote: knowledge of European history, even of English history, was superficial and her grasp of historical method was non-existent
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Norman Cohn, Europe's Inner Demons (1975), seen only at second hand through Wikipedia's citation; the book itself was not fetched
suggested_refs: The Queen Victoria Memorial Hospital, Welwyn village, Hertfordshire

stops.name: Golders Green, the funeral and the cremation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: one lens states flatly that no crematorium is named in its source, another gives Golders Green and this date on a Find a Grave memorial, which is user-compiled and weaker than the rest of this source base. The disagreement is not resolved
stops.campa: The funeral is held a week after the death and the body is cremated at Golders Green. No grave or headstone is documented anywhere. What became of the ashes is stated in no source that can be reached: scattered, interred, or kept, the record simply stops. She spent her working life excavating other people's burials, and argued that the dead of the English trials were the last members of a religion nobody had troubled to record. The disposition of her own remains is undocumented.
stops.quote: very little evidence to suggest that the accused witches were either devil-worshippers or members of a pagan fertility cult
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Keith Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971), seen only at second hand through Wikipedia's citation; the book itself was not fetched

stops.name: University College London, the bronze bust
stops.date_confidence: the bust and the named common room are attested; neither is dated in any reachable source, and 1964 is a placement after her death, not a recorded date
stops.campa: A bronze bust of her stands in the Institute of Archaeology, sculpted by Stephen Rickard and paid for by her former student Violet MacDermot; the college names the women's common room she campaigned for after her. Neither memorial is a grave. By the 1970s the witch-cult hypothesis is finished as history, and by then Wicca is a working religion in several countries. In 1996 Diane Purkiss argues that the men who demolished her had a bias of their own, and in 2013 Kathleen Sheppard writes the first full biography, framed as recovering an archaeologist buried under her mentor's name.
stops.quote: That this 'old religion' persisted secretly, without leaving any evidence, is, of course, possible, just as it is possible that below the surface of the moon lie extensive deposits of Stilton cheese. Anything is possible. But it is nonsense to assert the existence of something for which no evidence exists...
stops.quote_source: Jeffrey B. Russell and Brooks Alexander, A New History of Witchcraft: Sorcerers, Heretics and Pagans (London: Thames and Hudson, 2007), p. 42; seen at second hand through Wikipedia's citation. The circulating version of this passage gives the title without 'New' and stops mid-passage without an ellipsis
